messages:
Priya (Customer): Hi team — after we moved the app to the private subnet with PrivateLink, our calls to api.redwood.example keep getting 403s or time out. Happens from multiple instances. Started after the endpoint was created.
Sam (Support): Sorry you're hitting this, Priya. Can you paste the exact curl or SDK error and the VPC endpoint ID? Also are you using AWS Interface Endpoint (vpce) and Private DNS enabled?
Priya (Customer): curl returns 403 from host, sometimes connection reset. example:
```
$ curl -v https://api.redwood.example/v1/predict
* Connected to 10.10.5.20 (10.10.5.20) port 443 (#0)
> GET /v1/predict HTTP/1.1
> Host: api.redwood.example
> User-Agent: curl/7.68.0
>
< HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
< content-type: application/json
{ "error": "forbidden" }
```
VPCE ID: vpce-0abc1234
Private DNS: enabled
Sam (Support): Thanks — jumping in. Maria/Kevin: this looks like TLS/SNI or host header mismatch, or an egress/proxy returning 403. Customer says private DNS is enabled so traffic should hit the interface endpoint . ENI IP 10.10.5.20 matches that.
Maria (Eng): Quick checks: 1) Is the endpoint configured with the correct service name (com.amazonaws.vpce.redwood-inference)? 2) Any ALB/NLB in front of our service that might expect a specific SNI/Host? 3) Are there any inline WAF/proxy rules on the customer's path?
Priya (Customer): We created the endpoint via console -> Interface endpoint -> selected "com.redwood.inference.api" from marketplace. Security group attached is sg-0aa111. We have an outbound allowlist to Redwood maintained IP ranges in our firewall — could that be the issue?
Kevin (SRE): If they enabled Private DNS, DNS should resolve to the endpoint ENI. But if the firewall egress allowlist blocks Redwood's infrastructure IPs (or our public egress), then the endpoint may forward to a proxy that returns 403. Also check that the endpoint SG allows inbound 443 from the app subnets.
Sam (Support): Can you run these from one of the instances and paste results? 1) dig +short api.redwood.example 2) curl -vk --resolve "api.redwood.example:443:10.10.5.20" https://api.redwood.example/v1/ping 3) openssl s_client -connect 10.10.5.20:443 -servername api.redwood.example
Priya (Customer): running now, output:
```
$ dig +short api.redwood.example
10.10.5.20

$ curl -vk --resolve "api.redwood.example:443:10.10.5.20" https://api.redwood.example/v1/ping
* Connected to 10.10.5.20 (10.10.5.20) port 443 (#0)
* TLS 1.2 connection established
* Server certificate: CN=*.redwood.example
> GET /v1/ping HTTP/1.1
> Host: api.redwood.example
>
< HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
```
Priya (Customer): openssl shows the cert CN is *.redwood.example (ok). No obvious TLS errors.
Maria (Eng): Cert looks fine. 403 suggests an authorization layer in front of the endpoint rejecting the request — could be our routing policy expecting a different route or token header. Can you confirm the Authorization header used? Is the same client working from the public internet?
Priya (Customer): Same app deployed in another VPC with internet egress works fine and returns 200. We do include the same Bearer token.
Kevin (SRE): Two hypotheses: 1) PrivateLink route is hitting a different Redwood tenant/service (ownership mismatch) and RBAC blocks it. 2) The customer's NAT/proxy/firewall is mutating headers or stripping Auth. Also check that the SG on the endpoint allows return traffic (ephemeral ports) — sometimes SGs block ephemeral outbound and break TLS sessions.
Sam (Support): Also check the endpoint policy — if it's restricted to a set of principals, it might be denying the principal used from that account. Can you paste the vpce policy? Example: `aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoint --vpc-endpoint-ids vpce-0abc1234`
Priya (Customer): policy looks default (allow). SG allows outbound 0.0.0.0/0 and inbound from app subnet on 443. Our firewall egress allowlist is a proxy; I asked network ops to bypass proxy for that subnet to test.
DeployBot: Deployment vpce-0abc1234 updated: private-dns=true, security-groups=[sg-0aa111], subnet-ids=[subnet-0a,subnet-0b]
Priya (Customer): Bypassing proxy temporarily — same 403.
Maria (Eng): Ok that rules out proxy mutation. Next: can you curl with `-H "Host: api.redwood.example" -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"` and add `-v` show raw response headers. Also try hitting the endpoint IP with a different Host header like `example.invalid` to see if Host matters (we might be routing by virtual host).
Priya (Customer): When I call with wrong Host header I get `400` from the endpoint IP. With correct Host + token we still get 403. Raw response headers:
```
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
content-type: application/json
x-vpce-service: redwood-inference
x-proxy-node: gateway-7
x-request-id: r-9c3a
```
Kevin (SRE): x-vpce-service header confirms it hit our gateway. x-proxy-node indicates which edge. r-9c3a is our request id — Maria, can you look up request id r-9c3a in our logs for that time (2470012348)?
Maria (Eng): Looking — r-9c3a shows auth failure: token validated but tenant mismatch: incoming request claimed tenant id T-123 but endpoint mapped to tenant T-456. That explains 403. How is the tenant being set? Priya, do you have any custom host header rewriting or tenant header injection?
Priya (Customer): Our app sets `X-Tenant: T-123`. We assumed the token and tenant header should match. On internet path it does. Why would PrivateLink change mapping?
Sam (Support): PrivateLink itself shouldn't change headers. But our gateway routing might map vpce-0abc1234 to a specific customer routing table if the endpoint is set up under a particular AWS account or mapping. It sounds like the endpoint was provisioned under a different customer/partner account and is wired to a different tenant in our config.
Maria (Eng): Confirmed in config: vpce-0abc1234 is associated with customer account 789 and bound to tenant T-456 in our control plane. If Priya's tenant is T-123, the bound tenant is wrong — that's why token tenant mismatch. Resolution: rebind the VPCE mapping to the correct tenant or recreate the endpoint in the customer's account following our PrivateLink onboarding flow.
Kevin (SRE): Actionable steps:
- Priya: please share the account ID where the endpoint was created.
- Sam/Maria: we'll request a binding change to map vpce-0abc1234 -> tenant T-123.
- Quick mitigation: create a temporary route on the customer's side to reach the public endpoint (keeps traffic working) or recreate the VPCE under the expected account with correct service name.
Priya (Customer): Endpoint created in our account ID 111222333444. We expected on-boarding to auto-bind to T-123. How did it get bound to T-456?
Maria (Eng): Looks like during onboarding the wrong VPCE ID was provided to our provisioning UI and an ops engineer bound it to the wrong tenant. We'll unbind and rebind; ETA ~30m. We'll post updates.
Sam (Support): Sorry for the churn. I'll keep monitoring the request id stream for r-9c3a family and confirm when binding change completes. Meanwhile we've noted Docs update: instruct customers to verify vpce ID in onboarding step and include check `x-vpce-id` in request logs.
Priya (Customer): Thanks — appreciate the speedy investigation. We'll standby.
Maria (Eng): Rebind complete — vpce-0abc1234 now mapped to tenant T-123. Please retry.
Priya (Customer): Retried — success! 200 responses now. Thanks all :rocket:
Sam (Support): Great. Root cause: operator-bound VPCE mapping to wrong tenant. Postmortem item: validate onboarding flow + add a check that binding tenant == token tenant for incoming VPCE requests.
Priya (Customer): Fine by us. Leaving firewall/proxy tests for our internal follow-up. Thanks everyone :clap:
